section.title: More Proverbs of Solomon
section.sectionRationale: A new collection begins here, explicitly labeled 'additional proverbs of Solomon, copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah,' 25:1, a scribal school project centuries after Solomon that gathered and preserved royal wisdom for a new generation. This chapter opens with kings and courts and moves through vivid, image-rich proverbs on timing, self-control, and honest speech.
section.thesis: It is the glory of kings to search out what God conceals, and true wisdom is patient, restrained, and fitly spoken, since a word rightly timed is like apples of gold in silver settings, while pride, gossip, and a temper out of control leave a life like a city with broken walls.
section.frameNote: Five clusters: the glory of God and kings, and self-restraint before rulers; the fitly spoken word and the trustworthy messenger; kindness to an enemy and the danger of overexposure; honey in moderation and the danger of a quarrelsome tongue; self-control as the true wall of a life.

units.label: The glory of God and kings
units.note: concealing and searching out a matter

verses.text: These are additional proverbs of Solomon, which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah:
It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out.
As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, so the hearts of kings cannot be searched.
Remove the dross from the silver, and a vessel for a silversmith will come forth.
Remove the wicked from the king's presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness.
Do not exalt yourself in the presence of the king, and do not stand in the place of great men;
for it is better that he says to you, "Come up here!" than that you should be demoted in the presence of the prince. Even what you have seen with your own eyes,
do not bring hastily to court. Otherwise, what will you do in the end when your neighbor puts you to shame?

units.label: The fitly spoken word
units.note: apples of gold, the trustworthy messenger

verses.text: Argue your case with your neighbor without betraying another's confidence,
lest the one who hears may disgrace you, and your infamy never go away.
A word {{davar|fitly}} spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
Like an earring of gold or an ornament of fine gold is a wise man's rebuke to a listening ear.
Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a trustworthy messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters.
Like clouds and wind without rain is the man who boasts of gifts never given.

units.label: Patience, kindness to an enemy
units.note: coals of fire, burning coals of kindness

verses.text: Through patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break a bone.
If you find honey, eat just what you need, lest you have too much and vomit it up.
Seldom set foot in your neighbor's house, lest he grow weary and hate you.
Like a club or sword or sharp arrow is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor.
Like a broken tooth or a foot out of joint is confidence in a faithless man in time of trouble.
Like one who removes a garment on a cold day or vinegar poured on a wound is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.
If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink.
For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.

units.label: Honey, gossip, and self-control
units.note: a city whose walls are broken down

verses.text: As the north wind brings forth rain, so a backbiting tongue brings angry looks.
Better to live on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife.
Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land.
Like a muddied spring or a polluted well is a righteous man who gives way to the wicked.
It is not good to eat too much honey or to search out one's own glory.
Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who does not control his {{ruach|temper}}.

davar.gloss: Fitly spoken, literally 'a word upon its wheels' or in its proper setting. Verse 11 pictures such a word as apples of gold in silver settings, treasuring not just true speech but speech rightly timed and rightly placed, the same concern for timing that runs through the whole chapter.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, temper. Verse 28 pictures a man who cannot control his ruach as a city with broken walls, utterly exposed to attack; the same word elsewhere names the Spirit of God, showing how central self-mastery of one's inner spirit is to the whole biblical picture of wisdom.

basic.context: A new collection opens here, explicitly credited to Hezekiah's scribes who preserved older Solomonic proverbs generations later. The chapter moves from kings and courts, restraint before rulers, and honest testimony, through a string of vivid similes about well-timed words, patience, kindness to enemies, and finally self-control, pictured as the wall that keeps a life from being overrun.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter teaches largely through simile, 'like apples of gold,' 'like a broken tooth,' 'like a city with broken walls,' inviting the reader to feel the truth in a vivid image rather than merely accepting an abstract rule. As elsewhere in Proverbs, these are wise generalizations about how patience, honesty, and self-control tend to work, not legal guarantees for every situation.
basic.originalLanguages: The Hebrew phrase behind 'fitly spoken,' verse 11, literally means 'a word upon its wheels,' picturing speech that moves smoothly, rightly timed and rightly placed, like apples of gold nestled in silver settings. And ruach, spirit or temper, verse 28, pictures the self as a walled city, so that a person who cannot control this inner spirit stands defenseless, like a city whose walls have fallen.
basic.typology: Kindness to a hungry, thirsty enemy that heaps burning coals of shame and softening on his head, verses 21-22, anticipates Christ's command to love enemies and Paul's direct quotation of this proverb in Romans 12:20. The king's glory in searching out what God conceals, verse 2, foreshadows Christ, the greater Solomon, in whom all the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found, Colossians 2:3.
basic.christ: Paul directly quotes verses 21-22 in Romans 12:20, commanding believers to feed a hungry enemy and give a thirsty one drink, heaping burning coals on his head, showing that Christ's ethic of enemy love was already present, in seed form, in Solomon's wisdom, and now finds its full shape in the cross, where Christ loved and died for His enemies, Romans 5:10. And the chapter's praise of the king who searches out what is concealed, verse 2, points to Christ, the true king in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Colossians 2:3.
basic.god: It is God's own glory to conceal a matter, verse 2, leaving mystery even for kings to seek out, showing that not all things are meant to be immediately plain, and that the search for wisdom itself honors Him. He also rewards kindness shown to an enemy, verse 22, revealing a character concerned not merely with justice but with the possibility of an enemy's repentance and change.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 12:20 directly quotes verses 21-22 on kindness to an enemy. Colossians 2:3 echoes the hidden treasures a greater king searches out, verse 2. Matthew 5:44 develops love for enemies commanded here in seed form. James 3:2 echoes verse 28's concern for self-control as the mark of a mature life.
basic.oneStory: This chapter honors kings who search out God's hidden glory, prizes well-timed and honest speech, and commands kindness even toward enemies. All of this reaches its fullest form in Christ, the true king in whom wisdom's treasures are hidden, and whose own enemy love at the cross fulfills what this chapter could only sketch.

context.literary:
Proverbs 25 begins a second Solomonic collection, which runs through chapter 29, and the change in texture from chapters 10 to 22 is plain. Instead of balanced two line sayings that set the wise against the foolish, the opening movement is full of comparisons, 'like this, so that,' and many of them are strikingly concrete: apples of gold, snow at harvest, clouds without rain, a broken tooth, a muddied spring. The proverb of chapter 25 spends its energy on picture, and often asks the reader to work out where the picture bites.

The chapter falls into two halves that mirror each other. Verses 2 to 15 are a courtly half, concerned with kings, courts, neighbours, testimony and the art of persuasion. Verses 16 to 28 are a home and street half, concerned with moderation, hospitality, friendship, enemies and the guarded self. The two halves share a thread of restraint. The first opens with the king's duty to search things out and ends with the 'gentle tongue' that can break a bone, verse 15. The second opens with eating just enough honey and ends with the man whose temper has no wall, verse 28. Honey itself bookends the second half, verse 16 and verse 27, which makes appetite the key to self government.

There is also a movement from the king to the individual. The first verses place the monarch's glory in searching and in removing the wicked from his presence, so that justice rests on a clean court. By the end every listener is told that he is a city with a wall to guard. The idea of ruling is passed from the throne to the person, which is a lesson the book makes elsewhere, 16:32.

Several lines here repeat sayings found elsewhere in the book. Verse 24 is almost identical to 21:9, a reminder that Proverbs treats repetition as a form of emphasis, and that the same truth can be heard again in a new setting.
context.historical:
The heading in 25:1 is one of the few historical notes in the book. These proverbs were attributed to Solomon, yet copied out by 'the men of Hezekiah king of Judah,' about two and a half centuries later. Hezekiah's reign was a time of reform and recovery. The Chronicler says that in the first month of his first year he opened and repaired the doors of the temple, 2 Chronicles 29:3, and he restored worship, and he also prepared the city for siege by blocking the upper outlet of the Spring of Gihon and channelling the water into the city, 2 Chronicles 32:30. Under the same king the Assyrian threat reached Jerusalem's walls. It is a plausible setting for a scribal programme to gather the nation's inheritance of wisdom, though the text does not say why the scribes did it.

The chapter's royal sayings were meant for a court. 'The glory of kings to search it out,' 25:2, describes the royal task of investigating cases and counselling in secret, while 'the hearts of kings cannot be searched,' 25:3, is a frank admission that a ruler's mind is a closed matter to his subjects. The advice not to push forward in the king's presence, 25:6 to 7, fits a court where seating and access marked rank, and where humiliation in public could end a career.

The homely images come from village and household life. Snow in harvest, 25:13, would have been a rare relief in the hot dry months, perhaps a reference to snow brought from the mountains for drinks. The 'corner of the roof,' 25:24, was the flat roof of a house where one could sit in the open air. Refining silver, 25:4, was a familiar craft, with the dross lifted from molten metal, and the prophets use the same image of God purging His people, Isaiah 1:25. The walls of 25:28 recall that a city's walls were its life, and that broken walls meant helplessness, which is why Nehemiah wept when he heard of Jerusalem's, Nehemiah 1:3.
context.canonical:
The first verse is itself a canonical statement: it tells us that the Bible took shape through careful transmission. Scribes under a godly king gathered and copied earlier wisdom, and the Spirit-given text came to us through that human process. The wider statement, that glory belongs to God in what He conceals, joins Deuteronomy 29:29, 'The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us,' and Paul's cry that God's judgments are unsearchable and His ways untraceable, Romans 11:33. Jesus repeats the pattern when He thanks the Father for hiding things from the wise and revealing them to little children, Matthew 11:25.

The silver and the dross of 25:4 belong to a long line of refining language. God promises to purge Israel's dross, Isaiah 1:25, and Malachi says the Lord will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, Malachi 3:3. Paul uses the vessel image in 2 Timothy 2:20 to 21, where cleansing from what is unfit makes a vessel fit for the Master's use.

Verse 6 and 7 are the seedbed of Jesus's wedding banquet parable, Luke 14:7 to 11. The advice to wait for the host to say 'Come up here' becomes a rule of the kingdom: the humble will be exalted. The commands about enemies, 25:21 to 22, are quoted by Paul in Romans 12:20, and Jesus teaches the same spirit when He says to love your enemies, Matthew 5:44. The idea of good news from a distant land, 25:25, is taken up by Isaiah, 'How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news,' Isaiah 52:7, and by Paul, who says Christ 'came and preached peace to you who were far away,' Ephesians 2:17. The broken walls of 25:28 reach forward to Nehemiah, whose project was to rebuild a wall, Nehemiah 2:17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Hezekiah's scribes, and Solomon before them, wanted the court and the household to see that wisdom is learned by looking at the world and making comparisons. Almost every verse here asks the reader to hold two things side by side and see what each says about the other. A skilled word is like gold in silver; a boaster is like a sky that promises rain and gives none; a man with no hold on his temper is like a city with no wall. The teacher wants the hearer to learn by feeling the picture, not by memorising a rule.

The opening verses speak to those who hold power. The king's duty is to look into things that are not immediately plain, and to keep the court clean of the wicked, 25:4 to 5. The reader who is not a king still learns from this, because the same patience and care are asked of any who bear responsibility. The following verses train a younger person in humility before power, in discretion about secrets and in the reliability of a good messenger.

The second half presses for balance. Eat enough honey but not too much; visit a neighbour but not too often. The teacher is aiming at a character who understands limits, who can be kind to an enemy, who does not carry gossip, and who guards his own spirit. The final image of the broken wall leaves one question hanging before the reader: whether he has any defence against his own anger and appetite.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this chapter is observation in the form of simile, and it should not be read as law. 'Like clouds and wind without rain is the man who boasts of gifts never given' is a description that wants to be understood and avoided; it is not a statute. The imperatives that do appear, such as not hurrying to court, giving food to a hungry enemy, and eating honey in moderation, carry moral weight because they match the wider witness of Scripture, but they are still wisdom for the way of life, not rules for every case.

Two verses need care. The 'coals of fire' in 25:22 are paired with a promise that the LORD will reward, and Paul quotes them as a reason for believers to do good, Romans 12:20. The text does not give a licence to use kindness as a trick for hurting an enemy; Paul's next verse says to overcome evil with good. The remark about 'a quarrelsome wife' in 25:24 is a sorrowful description of a household in conflict, drawn from the male teacher's viewpoint, and the same book honours the wise woman and the excellent wife, 31:10 to 31. It does not justify treating a spouse as a problem, and the principle applies to any member of a household who makes peace impossible. What carries over is the invitation to examine ourselves: our speech, our timing, and our restraint.

debates.question: What are the 'burning coals' in 25:22?

views.label: Shame that leads to repentance
views.case: Kindness to an enemy makes him feel what he has done and so burns with remorse. Many commentators take this to be the sense, and see in Paul's next words, 'overcome evil with good,' Romans 12:21, the aim of changing the enemy and not harming him.

views.label: Added judgment on the unrepentant
views.case: Others read the coals as a symbol of the greater punishment that comes on an enemy who refuses the kindness, and see in Paul's context a warning to leave vengeance with God, Romans 12:19. The reward the LORD promises is then the justice He will do.

views.label: The pain of conscience as a refining fire
views.case: A third view stresses that the same image is used of a fire that purifies, as with silver in 25:4. The coals are an uncomfortable mercy, burning off hostility, and the aim is the restoration of the enemy.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the believer's part is to feed and give drink without malice. Whether the coals soften or judge is left to God, and Paul's command to overcome evil with good makes restoration the goal.

debates.question: What is the 'apple of gold' in 25:11?

views.label: A real fruit in a decorated setting
views.case: Some think of golden fruit, such as citrus or apricot, displayed in silver filigree or baskets. The point is that a well timed word is beautiful and valuable at once, and delights the eye as well as the hearer.

views.label: A work of the goldsmith
views.case: Others hold that the phrase names a crafted ornament, golden apples set in silver, in line with the next verse, which speaks of an earring of gold. Words are then precious because they are skilfully made.

debates.bearing: The identification of the object matters less than the point of the comparison: a word spoken at the right time, in the right way, adds beauty to a life, and its effect lasts. This is the teacher's way of saying that how and when we speak matters as much as what we say.

study.originalLanguages:
Several expressions in this chapter reward a slower reading. The first is the contrast in 25:2 between God and kings. God's glory lies in 'concealing' a matter, and the glory of kings lies in 'searching it out.' The two verbs belong to different stages of one picture. What God conceals is not a trick but a gift, a world and a word that are worth the effort of digging, and the king who digs honours the God who has hidden. The verb for searching is used elsewhere of searching out a matter in a legal investigation, and of God's own searching of hearts. It is therefore a verb for careful inquiry, not casual curiosity.

The second is the 'dross' of 25:4. The word means the impurities that rise to the top when silver is melted. The image is a continuous process: the refiner removes what is false, and what remains is a vessel fit for the silversmith. The next verse applies the process to the court: take the wicked from the king's presence and the throne stands firm in righteousness. Justice is a matter of refining the people around the throne.

Third, the description of the apt word in 25:11. The Hebrew says a word spoken 'upon its wheels,' or in its right circumstances, and translators differ over the exact sense. The traditional rendering is 'fitly spoken' or spoken in the right setting, and a number of scholars prefer 'spoken in season.' Either way the thought is of timing. The next verse repeats the sense with a wise rebuke given to 'a listening ear,' a reminder that the hearer must also be ready.

Fourth, the 'soda' of 25:20. The BSB footnote notes that the Hebrew can mean vinegar poured on soda, that is, on natron or alkali, which would produce a violent fizz. Whichever is intended, the image is of something that provokes and aggravates. The comparison with taking off a coat on a cold day makes the point: cheerful songs sung to a heavy heart add insult to sorrow.

Fifth, the word ruach in 25:28, 'spirit' or 'temper.' It is the same word used of breath, wind and the Spirit of God. Here it is the inner life of a person, and the verse says that where there is no restraint over it, there is no wall. The same idea is in 16:32, where the one who rules his spirit is better than a man who captures a city. The BSB footnote to 25:23 is also worth noting: the Hebrew of the first line can be taken as the north wind bringing rain or driving it away, and translators have gone both ways, though the meaning that slander brings angry looks fits either reading.

typology.type: The humble guest called up higher, Proverbs 25:6 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The advice to wait until the host says 'Come up here' is the root of Jesus's parable of the wedding banquet, where the one who takes the lowest place is told, 'Friend, move up to a better place,' Luke 14:10. Jesus then states the rule: 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted,' Luke 14:11. He lives it, for He 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death,' and therefore 'God exalted Him to the highest place,' Philippians 2:8 to 9. The proverb gives prudence; Christ gives the pattern and the power. It falls short as a type because the proverb's humility can be a tactic, while His was a real self giving.

typology.type: Silver purified of dross, Proverbs 25:4 to 5
typology.fulfillment: The silversmith removes the dross and the king removes the wicked, and the result is a vessel and a throne that stand firm. The prophets say that God will purge His people's dross, Isaiah 1:25, and Malachi says the Lord will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, Malachi 3:3. Christ is the royal refiner who purifies His own for Himself, Titus 2:14. The correspondence is real but it escalates: the dross that He removes is lodged within His people, and He bears it Himself on the cross. The earthly king can only remove people from his presence; Christ cleanses them and keeps them near.

typology.type: The kindness to an enemy, Proverbs 25:21 to 22
typology.fulfillment: The command to feed a hungry enemy is a seed that Christ grows into a tree. He taught, 'love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,' Matthew 5:44, and He showed it when 'we were enemies of God' and were 'reconciled to Him through the death of His Son,' Romans 5:10. The proverb gives a rule for a single hand; Christ gives Himself. The type falls short in motive. The proverb offers the LORD's reward for the kindness, while Christ's love was given when there was no merit and no prospect of repayment.

typology.type: Good news from a far country, Proverbs 25:25
typology.fulfillment: The picture of water to a tired traveller anticipates the gospel. Isaiah sings of the messenger whose feet are beautiful on the mountains as he proclaims peace, Isaiah 52:7, and Paul says Christ 'came and preached peace to you who were far away,' Ephesians 2:17. The refreshment is for those who were far from home, as the Gentiles were. The type falls short in that the proverb's news is a letter from a loved one, while the gospel is the arrival of the Son who comes to bring His people home. The messenger and the message become one person.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most plainly through the command about enemies. Paul quotes 25:21 to 22 in Romans 12:20, and then adds: 'Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good,' Romans 12:21. What Solomon's scribes wrote as a wise courtesy, the New Testament places in the centre of Christian life, because the church follows a Lord who has first done it. Paul says 'when we were enemies of God' we were 'reconciled to Him through the death of His Son,' Romans 5:10. We were the hungry and thirsty enemy, and He fed us. The coals of 25:22 are not a clever technique but a description of what love does to those who receive it. Christ overcame our hostility with good, and in that, the proverb finds its fullest sense.

The opening verse, about the glory of God in concealing a matter, leads to Christ as the unveiling. God has hidden wisdom through the ages and Paul calls it 'the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints,' Colossians 1:26. 'Christ in you, the hope of glory,' is how he states it in verse 27. In Christ 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,' Colossians 2:3, and the king who searches does not search in vain, because the hidden thing has come to be found. The rulers of this age did not understand it, or they would not have crucified the Lord of glory, 1 Corinthians 2:8. So the proverb speaks of a God who conceals, and the gospel says that in Christ He has opened what He hid, to those who come as little children, Matthew 11:25.

The humility saying of 25:6 to 7 is a signpost to Christ's own path. Jesus takes the proverb and lifts it into a parable of the kingdom, Luke 14:7 to 11, and then lives it to the cross, where He took the lowest place and was raised to the highest, Philippians 2:8 to 9. The faithful messenger who refreshes the soul of those who sent him, 25:13, brings Jesus to mind, who said, 'My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work,' John 4:34. And the good news from a distant land, 25:25, is the news He brought and is.

The last image, a man without a wall, shows the need. Our spirit has no defence of its own, and the New Testament lists self control as part of the fruit of the Spirit, Galatians 5:22 to 23. That is a gift from the one who ruled His own spirit perfectly. A caution remains. The chapter is not a coded prediction, and each saying is first of all practical. The links to Christ are the ones the New Testament makes, through the enemy, the hidden wisdom and the lowly guest.
study.god:
The chapter's first claim about God is a surprising one: concealment is part of His glory. A God who hides a matter is not being unkind. He has made a world and given a word that reward searching, so that human minds are made for discovery and the discovery gives Him honour. The same thought stands in Deuteronomy 29:29, where the secret things are His and the revealed things are ours. This shapes worship, because it asks for both humility and curiosity. We do not know all, and we are not meant to; but what is shown we are to hold and follow. Paul's cry at the end of his long argument in Romans, that God's judgments are unsearchable and His ways untraceable, Romans 11:33, is this verse at full volume.

It shows God as the one who sets the order of honour. The proverb warns against pushing into a king's presence, and Jesus makes the principle divine: the host decides who goes up, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted, Luke 14:11. Rank belongs to God and is not seized. His own exaltation of His Son came after humility, Philippians 2:9.

He is a God who rewards the kindness shown to an enemy, 25:22. The promise says that the LORD will reward, which tells us that He sees what is done in secret, such as giving bread to someone who hates us, and that He does not forget it. It also says something about His own heart. He fed His enemies with the gift of His Son, Romans 5:10, and delights when His people do likewise.

He is also the God who holds the limits of creaturely appetite. The honey proverbs, 25:16 and 25:27, treat good things as gifts that can be spoiled by excess. This agrees with a God who calls creation good, and who gives food for enjoyment, and who also asks for restraint, which He supplies by His Spirit, Galatians 5:23. The broken wall of 25:28 is a picture that a God of order uses to warn: a person who lacks self control is exposed.

Finally, He speaks in pictures. The very form of the chapter reflects His way of teaching: He uses silver, snow, clouds, wells and walls to say what a bare command could not. Worship therefore includes the habit of looking at created things and hearing His voice in them, and it includes patience with the long work of searching, since 'It is the glory of God to conceal a matter,' and He delights to be found.

crossReferences.note: The secret things belong to the LORD and the revealed things to His people. It states in a single line what 25:2 says in two: God keeps some things hidden and gives others, and our task is to search where He has opened the door and to obey what we are shown.

Paul ends his great argument about God's purposes with wonder at the depth of His wisdom and the unsearchable character of His judgments. It deepens 25:2 and 25:3: the king may search, but the full depth of God's ways is beyond anyone, and the right response is praise.

Jesus's parable of the wedding guests develops 25:6 to 7. He turns the prudence of waiting to be called up into a principle of the kingdom, and adds the promise that the humble will be exalted. It is a clear case of the Lord taking a proverb and showing its deepest ground.

Paul quotes 25:21 to 22 and sets it in a passage about leaving vengeance to God. He ends with the command to overcome evil with good. The cross-reference shows how the apostles read the proverb as part of a larger ethic of grace to those who harm us.

Jesus commands love for enemies and prayer for persecutors, because the Father gives sun and rain to the evil and the good. His teaching deepens 25:21 to 22 by grounding it in the Father's own character, not in the hope of making an enemy ashamed.

A gentle answer turns away wrath. It matches 25:15, where a gentle tongue can break a bone, and shows how the book uses a paradox: softness is stronger than hardness. Both verses say that persuasion works through patience and not through force.

Whoever controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city. This is the other half of 25:28's picture. The man without self control is a city with broken walls; the man who rules his spirit is stronger than the conqueror, because the greatest battle is within.

The messenger whose feet are beautiful on the mountains brings good news of peace and salvation. It stands behind 25:25, where good news from a distant land refreshes a weary soul, and it turns the proverb's comfort into the announcement of a reigning God.

Nehemiah calls the people to rebuild the broken wall of Jerusalem so that they will no longer be a disgrace. The ruined wall is a historical image of what 25:28 describes in a person, and the story shows that a broken wall can be rebuilt by people who set their hand to it.

The Lord sits as a refiner and purifier of silver, purifying the sons of Levi. It gives the divine side of 25:4 to 5: the removal of dross and the cleansing of those near the throne is God's own work, aimed at offerings given in righteousness.

study.oneStory:
The chapter draws on one of the Bible's oldest questions: how does a fallen people live under rulers, among neighbours and with their own hearts? The beginning of the Bible gave humanity the task of ruling creation under God, and the chapter's royal sayings recall that calling. The king's glory is to search out what God has hidden, which fits the first commission to subdue and to understand, Genesis 1:28. After the fall that task is hard and the rulers themselves are flawed, 'the hearts of kings cannot be searched.' Proverbs 25 therefore looks for a king whose heart can be trusted and whose court is cleansed of the wicked.

The chapter's note on Hezekiah is a sign of the story's movement. Hezekiah was among the better kings, and even he failed, Isaiah 39:1 to 8, so the nation's hope was not placed in him. The scribes kept the old wisdom for a future that would need it. The chapter's advice to a hearer in the presence of power, to wait for the call, is a pattern for people living under human rulers who are not yet the true king, and it points to the one who will say 'Come up here.'

In Christ the pattern is filled. He is the king who searches and the wisdom in whom hidden things are found, Colossians 2:3. He is the humble guest who becomes the host, and the Saviour who fed His enemies and overcame evil with good. He sends His people with the message of good news from the far country, Ephesians 2:17, and gives His Spirit so that the wall of self control can be built, Galatians 5:23. The picture of Nehemiah's rebuilt wall hints at this, a people restored under a leader who set his hand to the work.

The end of the story is the city whose walls are secure. Revelation describes a city with a great high wall, Revelation 21:12, whose gates are never shut, and in which nothing impure enters. The glory of God that is hidden now is revealed there: the city has no need of the sun because the glory of God gives it light, Revelation 21:23. The search that kings were set to do will end in sight, and those who sought wisdom as treasure will see it face to face.

quiz.q: According to verse 1, who preserved this collection of Solomon's proverbs?

options.text: The men of Hezekiah, king of Judah.
options.note: This chapter opens a new, explicitly credited collection copied generations after Solomon.

options.text: Solomon himself, writing them all at one time.
options.note: The proverbs originated with Solomon, but this collection specifically credits Hezekiah's scribes with copying them.

options.text: The prophet Isaiah.
options.note: Isaiah is not named as the source of this collection.

options.text: An unnamed group of anonymous scribes with no royal connection.
options.note: The scribes are specifically identified as working under King Hezekiah, not anonymous or unconnected to royal sponsorship.

quiz.q: What does verse 2 say is the glory of kings?

options.text: To search out a matter that it is God's glory to conceal.
options.note: Human rulers are given the dignity of investigation and discovery.

options.text: To conceal matters just as God does.
options.note: Concealing is specifically God's glory; searching out is the glory assigned to kings.

options.text: To rule with absolute, unquestioned power.
options.note: The verse's concern is searching out hidden matters, not raw power.

options.text: To avoid all difficult or mysterious questions.
options.note: This is nearly the opposite; the king's glory is precisely in pursuing what is concealed, not avoiding it.

quiz.q: What does verse 11 compare a word fitly spoken to?

options.text: Apples of gold in settings of silver.
options.note: Well-timed speech is prized as a rare and beautiful treasure.

options.text: A club or sharp arrow.
options.note: That image describes false testimony in verse 18, the opposite of a fitly spoken word.

options.text: Cold water to a weary soul.
options.note: That image describes good news from a distant land in verse 25, a related but distinct comparison.

options.text: Honey eaten in excess.
options.note: That image, from verse 27, warns against excess rather than praising fitly spoken words.

quiz.q: What does verse 21-22 instruct regarding a hungry or thirsty enemy?

options.text: Give him food and water, heaping burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.
options.note: Kindness to an enemy is commended and directly rewarded by God.

options.text: Refuse to help him until he apologizes first.
options.note: This is the opposite of what the verses command.

options.text: Report him to the authorities instead of helping.
options.note: The verses' focus is personal kindness, not a call to report the enemy.

options.text: Help him only if there is no risk to yourself.
options.note: The verses give an unconditional command to help, without this qualification.

quiz.q: What does verse 28 compare a man who does not control his temper to?

options.text: A city whose walls are broken down.
options.note: Lack of self-control leaves a person utterly exposed and defenseless.

options.text: A well-fortified city.
options.note: This is the opposite; the image is of a city defenseless due to broken walls.

options.text: A quiet, undisturbed garden.
options.note: This image does not appear in the verse.

options.text: A city with strong walls but no gate.
options.note: The verse's image is total exposure, broken walls entirely, not merely a missing gate.

questions: Verse 2 says it is the glory of kings to search out what God conceals. Where in your own life is God inviting patient searching rather than demanding instant answers?
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold, verse 11. Think of a recent conversation. Was your timing as wise as your words?
Verses 21-22 command kindness to a hungry or thirsty enemy. Who is someone that has wronged you whom you could practically bless this week?
Verse 17 warns against overstaying your welcome in a neighbor's house. Is there a relationship where you need to practice better boundaries, whether visiting too often or demanding too much?
Verse 28 pictures a person without self-control as a city with broken walls. Where is your own 'wall' down right now, in anger, appetite, or speech, leaving you exposed?

translationNotes.note: 'Copied by the men of Hezekiah' reflects a Hebrew verb for transcribing or compiling, evidence of an active scribal tradition preserving older wisdom material centuries after Solomon's reign.
'Fitly spoken' translates a rare Hebrew phrase, literally 'upon its wheels,' whose exact sense is debated but generally understood to mean rightly timed or aptly placed.

'Burning coals on his head' likely alludes to an ancient Egyptian penitential custom of carrying hot coals atop the head as a sign of shame and repentance, supporting a reading of transformative shame rather than vindictive punishment.
